More than 600 schools did not open this year because of security issues, according to the Afghanistan Education Ministry.  Watch what females face in Afghanistan » . It is a sentiment echoed by their principal, a 35-year veteran of Afghanistan's girls schools. "I am asking those who close schools and throw acid on girls to let the children of this country go to school because it's crime to close the schools, a crime against the children of this country," said Safia Hayat, principal of the Zarghona Girls School in Kabul. Hanafi, meanwhile, went on to discuss possible reconciliation talks with the Afghan government. "I don't think there can be any discussion of peace until the the foreigners leave Afghanistan," he said referring to the presence of coalition troops. Hanafi described himself as a commander in the southern province of Helmand, but announced a new Taliban offensive in the north was about to begin and that he would be playing a key role there.

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) — A senior Taliban commander has delivered a fresh warning to international aid employees, stating that the insurgent movement’s new “constitution” allows them either to kill such workers as spies or to detain them in order to trade them for imprisoned Taliban fighters.

In a Friday night telephone interview conducted exclusively with CNN, Mohammed Ibrahim Hanafi said the Taliban’s intelligence branch was working to collect information about foreign aid personnel. The interview lasted about 15 minutes and was organized through an intermediary.

“If we capture someone, this is how we will handle the case according to our new constitution,” Hanafi said. He also said he was urging “Afghan brothers” not to work for nongovernmental organizations.

During the interview, Hanafi reiterated the Taliban’s position that girls should be barred from public education. He said the movement’s rules had not changed from the period when it governed Afghanistan.

“Our law remains the same law that existed during our rule in Afghanistan,” he said. “Mullah Mohammad Omar was our leader, and he is still our chief and leader, so we will continue to follow the same law as before.”

Hanafi added that, in his view, the Taliban opposes girls attending school because it believes women should maintain their dignity by remaining at home rather than working as laborers for other people.

The start of Afghanistan’s new school year has been overshadowed by numerous attacks and crimes across the country, particularly acid assaults. Afghan schoolgirls have been randomly burned and scarred with acid as punishment for attending classes. According to Afghanistan’s Education Ministry, more than 600 schools failed to open this year because of security concerns.

Still, the schools that have opened have refused to back down. Young women told CNN that while they are afraid, they remain committed to gaining an education and improving their futures.

Their determination was echoed by Safia Hayat, principal of Kabul’s Zarghona Girls School and a 35-year veteran of girls’ education in Afghanistan.

“I ask those who shut schools and throw acid on girls to allow the children of this country to attend school, because closing schools is a crime — a crime against the children of this country,” Hayat said.

Hanafi also addressed the possibility of reconciliation talks with the Afghan government. Referring to coalition forces, he said he did not believe peace discussions could take place until foreign troops left Afghanistan.

Although his comments appeared to acknowledge that some reconciliation discussions were under way, Hanafi questioned what sort of peace could be achieved while Afghans were still being killed in NATO airstrikes.

Hanafi identified himself as a commander in the southern province of Helmand, but said a new Taliban offensive in northern Afghanistan was about to start and that he would have a major role in it.

His remarks point to the growing risks faced by humanitarian organizations operating in Afghanistan, where aid staff have long worked under difficult and dangerous conditions.

Under that framework, he indicated that the group remains opposed to girls attending school, reinforcing fears that the Taliban would again seek to restrict education for women and girls in areas under its influence. During the Taliban’s previous rule in Afghanistan, girls were largely barred from formal schooling, and women faced severe limits on work, movement, and public life.

The comments come amid an already volatile security environment for both aid workers and students. Humanitarian organizations have been targeted by insurgent groups, accused of supporting foreign interests, or caught in the broader conflict between militants, Afghan authorities, and international forces. Threats to treat aid workers as spies could further undermine relief efforts, particularly in rural areas where communities depend on outside assistance for health care, food, education, and emergency support.

Girls’ schools have also faced repeated intimidation and violence, including threats against teachers, attacks on school buildings, and efforts to frighten families away from sending daughters to class. Despite these dangers, many Afghan students, parents, and educators have continued to push for education. In numerous communities, girls still attend school, teachers continue their work, and local leaders attempt to protect classrooms from attacks and political pressure.

Hanafi’s remarks underscore the stakes of Afghanistan’s ongoing struggle over education, humanitarian access, and basic rights. For aid organizations, the threat of kidnapping, execution, or prisoner exchanges raises urgent questions about staff safety and the ability to deliver assistance. For Afghan girls, the Taliban’s position signals the persistence of ideological opposition to their education, even as many remain determined to study.

The interview serves as a reminder that Afghanistan’s conflict is not only being fought with weapons, but also through competing visions of society. On one side are forces seeking to impose strict controls on women, education, and foreign assistance; on the other are families, teachers, aid workers, and students trying to preserve access to learning and humanitarian support despite insecurity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article from Kabul about a Taliban commander threatening foreign aid workers and reaffirming bans on girls' education in Afghanistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**Kabul, Afghanistan (CNN)** — A senior Taliban commander has threatened foreign aid workers operating in Afghanistan and reaffirmed the group’s restrictions on girls’ education, deepening concerns among humanitarian organizations already struggling to deliver assistance in one of the world’s worst crises.

Speaking at a gathering in Kabul, the commander warned international aid groups that their activities would face “consequences” if they were deemed to violate Taliban rules, according to attendees and local media reports. He also reiterated the Taliban’s position barring most girls from attending secondary school and women from university, saying the restrictions would remain in place until further notice.

CNN could not independently verify the full remarks. Taliban officials have not publicly responded to requests for clarification.

The comments come as Afghanistan faces widespread poverty, food insecurity and a collapsing public health system. Since retaking power in August 2021, the Taliban has imposed sweeping limits on women and girls, including bans on female students in higher education and severe restrictions on women working for non-governmental organizations and the United Nations.

Humanitarian groups say the restrictions have sharply hampered aid delivery, particularly to women and children, who often can only be reached by female staff in conservative communities.

A Kabul-based aid worker, who asked not to be named for security reasons, said the latest remarks had intensified fears among international and Afghan staff.

“Every new threat makes it harder to operate,” the aid worker said. “We are here to provide food, medicine and basic services, but the environment is becoming more unpredictable.”

The United Nations has repeatedly called on the Taliban to reverse its policies on women and girls, warning that Afghanistan’s isolation will deepen as long as half the population is excluded from education and public life.

Taliban leaders have claimed their policies are based on their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture, while saying they seek international recognition and engagement. No country has formally recognized the Taliban government.

Rights groups say the education bans are among the most damaging measures imposed since the Taliban returned to power, depriving millions of girls of schooling and threatening the country’s long-term future.

“Afghanistan cannot recover while girls are denied education and women are pushed out of public life,” one international rights advocate said. “Threatening aid workers only worsens the suffering of ordinary Afghans.”

**Taliban commander says NGOs must accept restrictions, girls’ schools remain tied to “Islamic conditions,” and warns of spring offensive**

**KABUL —** Taliban commander Mohammed Ibrahim Hanafi has defended the movement’s restrictions on aid organizations and girls’ education, dismissed current reconciliation efforts as insufficient, and warned that Taliban forces are preparing a new offensive if negotiations fail to produce what he described as an “Islamic system.”

In an interview, Hanafi said international and Afghan non-governmental organizations would be allowed to operate only if they complied with Taliban rules and avoided activities the group considers contrary to its interpretation of Islam. He accused some NGOs of serving foreign interests, though he offered no evidence to support the claim.

“We are not against assistance to the Afghan people,” Hanafi said, according to the interview. “But aid work must respect our culture, our religion and the decisions of Islamic authorities.”

His comments come amid ongoing concerns from humanitarian agencies that restrictions on staff, monitoring and programming have limited aid delivery in parts of Afghanistan. Aid groups have repeatedly warned that political interference and limits on female workers can prevent vulnerable women and children from receiving essential services.

On girls’ education, Hanafi said the Taliban’s position was not opposition to schooling itself, but to what he called “un-Islamic” conditions in some schools. He said girls’ schools could operate where separate classrooms, female teachers and approved curricula were available.

“Education for girls is possible when it is within the framework of Sharia,” he said. “The problem is not education. The problem is the environment and the curriculum.”

Rights advocates and education officials have long criticized Taliban restrictions on girls’ schooling, saying such rules have often resulted in closures, intimidation of teachers and students, and the denial of education to large numbers of girls. International organizations have said access to education is a basic right and have urged all parties to protect schools from political and military pressure.

Hanafi also addressed reconciliation talks, saying the Taliban would not accept negotiations that required fighters to surrender or recognize a political order backed by foreign powers. He said talks could only succeed if foreign troops withdrew and if the movement’s demands for an Islamic system were taken seriously.

“If they want peace, they must listen to the real demands of the Afghan people,” he said. “Reconciliation cannot mean that we lay down our weapons while the occupation and corruption continue.”

Afghan government representatives and international mediators have previously said any settlement must include a ceasefire, constitutional protections and guarantees for women’s rights. Taliban leaders have often rejected those conditions or described them as issues to be addressed after a broader political agreement.

Hanafi further claimed that Taliban fighters were preparing for a renewed offensive, describing it as a response to military pressure and stalled negotiations. He did not provide verifiable details, and the claims could not be independently confirmed.

Security analysts say such statements are often intended to project strength ahead of negotiations or seasonal fighting periods. They also warn that threats of renewed attacks raise the risk to civilians, who have borne the heaviest cost of Afghanistan’s decades of conflict.

The interview underscores the continuing divide between the Taliban’s political and military leadership and those seeking a negotiated settlement. While Hanafi suggested the movement remains open to talks, his comments on education, aid organizations and military action indicate that major obstacles remain.

Humanitarian groups, women’s rights advocates and diplomats are likely to view the remarks as a sign that any future agreement would need enforceable guarantees on civilian protections, education and aid access. Meanwhile, communities in contested areas remain exposed to both battlefield violence and restrictions imposed by armed groups.

counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan —** Foreign aid organizations in Afghanistan are facing renewed threats from Taliban authorities and affiliated local commanders, according to aid workers and community leaders, as reports of intimidation against girls seeking education continue to rise in several provinces.

The pressure comes amid an already severe humanitarian crisis, with millions of Afghans dependent on food assistance, medical support, and basic education programs run by international and Afghan nongovernmental organizations.

Several aid workers in Kabul and eastern Afghanistan, speaking on condition of anonymity due to security concerns, said they had received warnings in recent weeks to halt programs involving women and girls. Some said local Taliban officials demanded staff lists, questioned female employees, or ordered organizations to limit services unless they complied with strict gender restrictions.

“We are trying to keep clinics open and distribute food, but every day the rules change,” one international aid coordinator said. “The threats are not always formal. Sometimes it is a phone call, sometimes a visit by armed men, sometimes a letter telling us we will be responsible for the consequences.”

Taliban officials have repeatedly said they are enforcing Islamic law and maintaining security, while denying that aid agencies are being deliberately targeted. A spokesman for the Taliban-led administration in Kabul said organizations must “respect Afghan values” and coordinate with local authorities.

But educators and rights advocates say the restrictions have created an atmosphere of fear — particularly for girls attempting to continue their studies despite bans on secondary and university education for female students.

In Kabul, several teachers described a growing network of informal classes held in private homes, basements, and community spaces. These classes, often staffed by former schoolteachers and university lecturers, provide lessons in math, science, literature, and English to girls who are no longer allowed to attend formal schools.

“Education has become something we whisper about,” said a teacher in western Kabul. “The girls arrive at different times so neighbors do not notice. They hide their books under scarves or inside shopping bags.”

Reports from local activists indicate that girls traveling to clandestine classes have been harassed at checkpoints and, in some cases, assaulted by unknown attackers. In one recent incident described by residents, a group of teenage girls was stopped on their way to a private lesson and threatened for carrying notebooks. In another, a small learning center was reportedly raided and shut down.

Cable-news crews and international journalists have limited access outside Kabul, making many accounts difficult to independently verify. Still, multiple humanitarian workers say the pattern is consistent: girls’ education programs are being pushed further underground, while those who support them are increasingly at risk.

At a quiet school building in Kabul that once served hundreds of girls, classrooms now sit empty. A former principal, who asked not to be named, said teachers still gather privately to discuss ways to keep their students learning.

“We spent twenty years telling girls they had a future,” she said. “Now they ask us, ‘What did we do wrong?’ We have no answer except to keep teaching however we can.”

International aid groups warn that threats against foreign and Afghan staff could force them to suspend operations in areas where needs are most acute. Afghanistan remains one of the world’s largest humanitarian emergencies, with widespread poverty, food insecurity, and a struggling health system worsened by economic isolation and reduced foreign funding.

The United Nations and human rights organizations have repeatedly called on Taliban authorities to lift restrictions on women’s education and employment, arguing that the policies harm not only women and girls but the entire country.

In Kabul, educators say the cost is already visible.

“When a girl is kept from school, a family loses a doctor, a teacher, an engineer, maybe a leader,” said one longtime instructor. “Afghanistan cannot rebuild itself while half of its children are locked out of the classroom.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an international news piece in the style of CNN about the Taliban’s “new constitution,” treatment of aid workers as spies, and continued opposition to girls’ education.
counterfactuals.output:
**Taliban signals hardline vision with proposed “new constitution,” escalating pressure on aid workers and continued ban on girls’ education**

*Kabul, Afghanistan —* The Taliban is seeking to further entrench its rule in Afghanistan through a proposed “new constitution” rooted in its interpretation of Islamic law, while intensifying scrutiny of humanitarian workers and maintaining restrictions that have kept most teenage girls and women out of classrooms and universities.

Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban has ruled Afghanistan largely by decree, dismantling many of the legal and political institutions established over the previous two decades. While the group has repeatedly promised governance based on Islamic principles, it has not produced a widely recognized constitutional framework accepted by Afghanistan’s political, ethnic and civil society groups — nor by the international community.

Rights advocates say any Taliban-backed constitution risks formalizing a system that excludes women from public life, limits political participation and suppresses dissent.

“The concern is not simply what is written on paper, but how the Taliban has governed in practice,” one Kabul-based civil society activist said, speaking anonymously for fear of reprisals. “Their policies already show what kind of state they want.”

The Taliban has defended its rule, saying it has restored security after decades of war and that its decisions are guided by Afghan culture and Islamic law. But no country has formally recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s legitimate government, and its treatment of women and girls remains a central obstacle to diplomatic engagement.

### Aid workers under suspicion

Humanitarian organizations operating in Afghanistan say their work has become increasingly difficult as Taliban authorities place growing restrictions on staff, movement and programming. Aid workers — particularly those linked to international organizations — have faced questioning, detention and accusations of espionage, according to humanitarian officials and rights groups.

The Taliban has frequently accused foreign-backed groups of attempting to undermine Afghanistan’s sovereignty or promote values it considers un-Islamic. Those allegations have contributed to a climate of fear among Afghan aid workers, many of whom are trying to deliver food, medical care and emergency support in one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.

International agencies say millions of Afghans remain in need of assistance, with poverty, unemployment and malnutrition widespread after years of conflict, economic collapse and international isolation.

Aid groups warn that branding humanitarian workers as spies could disrupt lifesaving operations.

“Humanitarian work depends on trust and access,” a senior aid official familiar with operations in Afghanistan said. “When staff are intimidated or accused of political activity, it becomes much harder to reach the people who need help most.”

The Taliban has also imposed restrictions on Afghan women working for NGOs and the United Nations, a move that aid agencies say has severely hampered programs serving women and children. In conservative communities, female staff are often essential for delivering assistance to women who cannot interact freely with male workers.

### Girls’ education still blocked

The Taliban’s continued opposition to girls’ secondary and higher education remains one of its most controversial policies.

Girls have been barred from most secondary schools since 2021, and women were later banned from universities. Despite repeated Taliban assurances that restrictions were temporary and would be reviewed, there has been no broad reopening of classrooms for older girls.

The policy has drawn condemnation from Muslim-majority countries, human rights organizations and the United Nations, which has described the restrictions as part of a broader system of gender-based discrimination.

For Afghan families, the impact has been devastating.

“My daughter asks me why her brothers can study and she cannot,” said a father in northern Afghanistan, who asked not to be named. “I have no answer.”

Some underground schools and online learning networks continue to operate, but teachers and students face risks. Activists say the longer the ban continues, the more Afghanistan’s future workforce — especially in health care, education and public administration — will be weakened.

The Taliban has argued that education for girls must conform to its standards on curriculum, dress and segregation, but critics say the group has used those conditions to indefinitely delay reopening schools.

### A government seeking legitimacy

The Taliban’s push for a more defined constitutional order comes as it seeks international legitimacy while resisting foreign pressure on human rights. Diplomats say engagement with the Taliban remains necessary to address terrorism concerns, migration, narcotics and humanitarian needs — but recognition is unlikely without major changes, especially on women’s rights.

Analysts say a Taliban constitution could become a tool for consolidating power rather than building an inclusive state.

“A constitution is supposed to limit power and protect citizens,” said an Afghanistan analyst based outside the country. “If it simply codifies Taliban decrees, it will deepen Afghanistan’s isolation.”

For now, Afghans remain caught between an unrecognized government seeking permanence and a humanitarian emergency with few signs of easing. For women and girls, aid workers and civil society activists, the message from Taliban rule has been unmistakable: the space to learn, work and speak freely continues to shrink.

Below is a **fictional, news-style draft** based on historical context. It should not be treated as a verified breaking-news report.

---

**KABUL — Taliban Signals Openness to Talks as Fear Lingers Over Acid Attacks on Schoolgirls**

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** A Taliban commander in eastern Afghanistan said Tuesday that insurgent leaders were prepared to consider renewed peace talks with the Afghan government, even as human rights advocates warned that any political settlement must protect girls’ education after years of attacks targeting female students and teachers.

Speaking by phone from an undisclosed location, the Taliban commander, who identified himself only as **Mawlawi Hamid**, said the movement was “not opposed to dialogue” if talks addressed foreign influence, prisoner releases and the future shape of Islamic governance.

“We have always said that war is not our first choice,” Hamid said. “If Kabul is serious and if the other side stops using talks as a tactic, then discussions can happen. But the rights of the Afghan people must be defined according to Islamic principles.”

Afghan government officials in Kabul did not immediately confirm whether formal negotiations were under way. A senior government aide, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to brief reporters, said intermediaries had been exploring “channels for communication,” but cautioned that any negotiations would require guarantees that the Taliban would cease attacks on civilians.

“The Afghan people want peace, but not at the cost of returning to fear,” the aide said. “Schools, hospitals and public life must be protected.”

The remarks come amid renewed anxiety among families in Kabul and provincial cities over the fate of girls’ education — one of the most visible and politically charged issues in any possible settlement with the Taliban.

### Legacy of Acid Attacks

Afghanistan has witnessed several attacks over the past two decades in which schoolgirls were targeted with acid or other chemicals, incidents that shocked the country and drew international condemnation. One of the most notorious occurred in **Kandahar in 2008**, when men on motorcycles threw acid at teenage girls walking to school, injuring several and leaving some with severe burns to their faces and hands.

At the time, Afghan authorities blamed militants opposed to female education. Taliban spokesmen denied involvement in some incidents, but rights groups said the broader climate of intimidation — including threats, school burnings, poisonings and attacks on teachers — was part of a campaign by extremists to keep girls out of classrooms.

For many Afghan families, those attacks remain a symbol of the risks girls face simply by seeking an education.

“Every time there is talk of a deal, mothers ask the same question: Will our daughters be safe?” said **Shukria Rahimi**, a Kabul-based women’s rights advocate. “Peace cannot mean silence for women. It cannot mean closing the school gates.”

In Kabul’s Dasht-e-Barchi neighborhood, where many families have endured years of violence, parents said they were watching developments with both hope and suspicion.

“We are tired of war,” said **Farzana**, a 37-year-old mother of three daughters. “But if peace means my girls must stay home, then what kind of peace is it?”

### Taliban Position Under Scrutiny

The Taliban commander interviewed Tuesday rejected accusations that the movement supports attacks on girls.

“Throwing acid on students is a crime,” Hamid said. “If someone does this, they should be punished. But the West uses these stories to insult the Islamic Emirate.”

Asked whether girls should be allowed to attend secondary school and university, he gave a more guarded answer.

“Education is permitted if it is in a safe environment and according to Islamic values,” he said. “The details must be decided by scholars and Afghan society, not foreigners.”

That formulation has alarmed activists, who say vague promises have often preceded restrictions on women’s public life.

“Language matters,” Rahimi said. “When commanders say ‘Islamic environment’ but do not clearly guarantee girls’ right to study, families hear a warning.”

### Peace Talks: Hope and Risk

Any possible negotiations would face major obstacles. Previous attempts at peace talks have collapsed over ceasefire violations, disputes over constitutional rights, prisoner exchanges and the role of international actors. The Afghan government has historically insisted that any peace process preserve the constitution, elections and civil rights protections, while the Taliban has demanded a governing system rooted more explicitly in its interpretation of Islamic law.

Analysts say both sides may have incentives to explore talks, especially after years of costly conflict and pressure from regional powers seeking stability. But they also warn that public trust remains fragile.

“Peace talks in Afghanistan are never just about ending gunfire,” said **Haroun Waziri**, a Kabul political analyst. “They are about power, legitimacy and the future of society — especially women’s rights and education.”

Waziri said acid attacks and other assaults on schoolgirls would inevitably shape public reaction to any Taliban role in governance.

“These crimes are not forgotten,” he said. “For many Afghans, they represent the fear that political compromise could erase hard-won freedoms.”

### Government Seeks Guarantees

Officials in Kabul have suggested that any agreement must include mechanisms to protect civilians, maintain access to education and prevent reprisals against former government workers, journalists and activists.

“Words are not enough,” the senior government aide said. “There must be monitoring, enforcement and consequences.”

International diplomats have also emphasized that aid and recognition could depend on the treatment of women and girls. Afghanistan’s education system remains heavily dependent on donor support, and many schools — particularly in rural areas — have struggled with insecurity, poverty and shortages of teachers.

For students, the political arguments feel immediate and personal.

“I want to become a doctor,” said **Laila**, a 15-year-old student in Kabul. “I hear adults talk about peace, but I want them to remember us. We are not politics. We are students.”

As rumors of possible talks spread through Kabul, the city remained tense but cautiously hopeful. For families who have lived through bombings, assassinations and attacks on classrooms, peace is desperately desired — but many say it must be peace with safeguards.

“We have buried too many children,” Farzana said. “Let them talk. Let them make peace. But do not bargain away our daughters’ future.”
